terms.definition: Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud — AWS's service for creating and managing virtual servers (instances) in the cloud.
terms.example: Like renting a computer in Amazon's data center instead of buying your own.

terms.definition: Amazon Machine Image — a software configuration template containing the OS, libraries, utilities, and pre-installed applications for an EC2 instance.
terms.example: Choosing Ubuntu as your AMI is like choosing which OS disc to install on a new laptop.

terms.definition: Defines the hardware configuration of an EC2 instance — specifically the number of virtual CPUs, RAM, and storage options.
terms.example: t2.micro = 1 vCPU, 1 GB RAM. Like choosing a laptop model based on its specs.

terms.definition: Elastic Block Storage — AWS's virtual hard drive service used as the storage disk for EC2 instances. Default size is 8 GB.
terms.example: Like the hard drive in your laptop, but cloud-based and resizable on demand.

terms.definition: A virtual stateful firewall that controls inbound and outbound network traffic for EC2 instances using rules based on protocol, port, and source IP.
terms.example: Like a security guard at the door — only people with the right badge (protocol/port) are let in.

terms.definition: Two cryptographically linked files — a public key stored on the EC2 instance and a private key kept on the user's local machine — used for SSH authentication instead of passwords.
terms.example: Like a padlock (public key) installed on the server door and your personal key (private key) to open it.

terms.definition: Secure Shell — a network protocol that allows encrypted, secure remote login and command execution on a remote computer. Uses port 22 by default.
terms.example: Like calling someone's phone (the server) to talk securely — SSH is the call protocol.

terms.definition: SSH Daemon — a background service on Linux servers that continuously listens on port 22 for incoming SSH connection requests.
terms.example: Like a receptionist always sitting at the desk, ready to verify visitors (SSH clients).

terms.definition: A program that interfaces between the user and the operating system — it receives commands, interprets them, and passes them to the OS via utilities.
terms.example: Like a translator between you and your OS — you speak shell language, the OS speaks machine language.

terms.definition: Command Line Interface — a text-based interface where users interact with the OS by typing commands in a terminal, rather than clicking visual elements.
terms.example: Typing 'mkdir project' to create a folder vs right-clicking in Windows Explorer.

terms.definition: Graphical User Interface — a visual, icon-based interface where users interact with the OS by clicking, dragging, and using menus.
terms.example: Windows Explorer, macOS Finder — visual interfaces for file management.

terms.definition: Bourne Again Shell — the default command-line shell on most Linux distributions, including Amazon Linux. Used to type and run commands.
terms.example: When you SSH into an EC2 instance and see a $ prompt, you're in a Bash shell.

terms.definition: Microsoft's command-line shell and scripting language for Windows, built on .NET. More powerful than the older Command Prompt.
terms.example: Like Bash for Linux, but for Windows — type commands to manage the OS and files.

terms.definition: Infrastructure as a Service — a cloud model where the provider manages physical hardware and virtualization, and the user manages OS, software, and configuration.
terms.example: EC2 is IaaS — AWS gives you a virtual machine; you install and manage everything on it.

terms.definition: An internet-accessible IP address assigned to your EC2 instance so external users and services can reach it. Changes each time you stop and restart an instance.
terms.example: Like your home address — other people on the internet can send traffic to this address.

terms.definition: An IP address only accessible within the AWS internal network (VPC). Used for communication between AWS resources.
terms.example: Like an internal office phone extension — only reachable from within the same building (VPC).

terms.definition: Rivest–Shamir–Adleman — an encryption algorithm used to generate EC2 key pairs. Creates two mathematically linked keys: public and private.
terms.example: Like a one-way trapdoor — easy to encrypt with the public key, only decryptable with the private key.

terms.definition: Privacy Enhanced Mail — a file format for storing private keys, used by OpenSSH and modern Windows SSH clients (Command Prompt, PowerShell).
terms.example: When you download a key pair with .pem format, you use it with the native 'ssh' command.

terms.definition: PuTTY Private Key — a file format for private keys used specifically by the PuTTY SSH client on Windows. Not compatible with OpenSSH.
terms.example: If you use PuTTY to connect, download your key in .ppk format instead of .pem.

terms.definition: HTTP Daemon — the Apache web server service that runs in the background on Linux and serves web content (HTML files) over HTTP on port 80.
terms.example: Install httpd on EC2, start it, place your HTML in /var/www/html/, and your website is live.

terms.definition: 'Superuser Do' — a Linux command prefix that runs the following command with administrator (root) privileges.
terms.example: 'sudo yum install httpd' installs Apache with admin rights even when logged in as ec2-user.

terms.definition: Permanently deleting an EC2 instance and its root EBS volume. Cannot be undone. Stops all compute charges.
terms.example: Like returning a rental car — once you do it, it's gone. Don't terminate unless you're done.

terms.definition: Temporarily pausing an EC2 instance — compute billing stops, but EBS storage billing continues. The instance can be restarted.
terms.example: Like turning off your laptop — files stay on the hard drive, ready to resume.
